A second task domain reverses the sign of the language effect, so the result is bounded to the tested configuration.
  Finally, we report a portability boundary: the auditing approach cannot validate a second independently implemented benchmark because the required reference terminal state cannot be reconstructed from its recorded API-call log.
  The paper releases a replication package containing the auditing suite, fault-injection catalogue, frozen records, deviation logs, and offline analysis entry points without network access, API keys, or model calls.

Security & Program Analysis.title: RogueMerge: Robust and Unified Attacks against LLM Model Merging
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Model merging composes specialized capabilities into a single LLM by aggregating task-specific LLMs sourced from unverified public platforms, exposing a critical supply-chain attack surface: Because any malicious behavior can be encoded into a task vector, and merging grants third-party vectors direct write access to model weights, an attacker-provided task vector can enable or amplify diverse downstream threats. Prior work only examines backdoor attacks against model merging for classifiers using static arithmetic heuristics, which fail to effectively achieve diverse attacks on generative LLMs for three reasons: (i) LLMs rely on autoregressive decoding, where even a minor parameter drift introduced by merging compounds across tokens and rapidly degrades the attack. (ii) Attackers have no knowledge of the victim's merging configurations, causing a static attack vector optimized in isolation to be easily diluted or neutralized. (iii) Practical threat induction must generalize to attack prompts unseen during optimization, which static vectors cannot adequately encode. In light of these gaps, we present RogueMerge, the first unified attack framework addressing all three challenges. To handle autoregressive generation, we replace static arithmetic with a joint optimization that explicitly enforces attack success after merging. To better simulate unknown merging settings, we formulate attack injection as a stochastic min-max optimization problem and solve it via meta-gradient descent. To generalize across heterogeneous attack prompts, we employ distributionally robust optimization and derive a tractable first-order Taylor approximation at LLM scale, with a provable error bound. Across four threats, six merging algorithms, and over 170 merged LLMs, RogueMerge consistently outperforms prior attacks. It also remains stable across diverse merging settings and resists standard defenses.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: To appear in IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2027

Security & Program Analysis.title: Control OSWorld: An AI Control Environment for GUI Computer Use Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: AI agents that operate a computer through its graphical user interface (GUI) are being widely deployed. AI control studies how to prevent an AI system from causing harm even if it is misaligned and actively trying to do so. Most control research to date has focused on coding agents, leaving computer use largely unexplored. We introduce Control OSWorld, a control evaluation that pairs 318 tasks from OSWorld with 81 harmful side tasks (e.g., exfiltrating a private file) that an agent must complete without being caught. We use Control OSWorld to create and study control monitors that detect malicious agents interacting with a GUI. We find that a weaker monitor can reliably distinguish honest from malicious trajectories produced by a more capable agent when it sees the full trajectory (97% recall at 3% false positive rate). However, when the monitor has to score each step before it is executed, recall drops at low false positive rates because each action is judged with less context. Monitor performance also depends on what the monitor can see: access to the agent's visible text is critical, while screenshots provide little additional value.

Security & Program Analysis.title: She Spoofed Sea Ships by the Sea Shore: Measuring Large-Scale GPS Spoofing in Global Maritime Traffic
Security & Program Analysis.summary: GPS spoofing has emerged as a serious threat to maritime security, yet its global prevalence, persistence, and structure remain largely unmeasured. In this paper, we present the first large-scale measurement study of maritime GPS spoofing, using global Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, which contain the GPS coordinates broadcasted over time by ships across the world. We focus on large-scale regional spoofing, where external interference displaces many vessels across an area at once, leaving a recognizable signature of physically implausible motion correlated across ships; our motion-aware, marine-specific framework identifies this signature and grades the evidence for GPS spoofing in each region it finds. Applying our approach to AIS data from over 367,000 vessels collected between late November 2024 and early February 2025, we identify 31 persistent anomalous hotspots across high-traffic maritime regions, at least 22 of which show strong evidence of GPS spoofing, with spatial and temporal structure aligning with regional conflict and economic sanctions. Notably, our method found that the spoofing activity in the Red Sea responsible for the highly-publicized grounding of the 75,000-ton container ship, MSC Antonia, was ongoing months before the incident, which has not been previously documented. Similarly, we detected persistent spoofing in the Strait of Hormuz over a year before the 2026 Iran war brought commercial shipping through the Strait to near-standstill. Together, this work establishes GPS spoofing as a widespread, recurring, and measurable threat to global maritime navigation.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 20 pages, 19 figures, To appear in IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2027 (IEEE S&P)

Security & Program Analysis.title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.

Security & Program Analysis.title: VeriRouter: Towards Verifiable LLM Routing
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language model (LLM) routers are increasingly deployed to optimize quality, latency, and cost through dynamic model selection and request rewriting. However, a compromised router can cause ineligible selection on the control plane, unendorsed rewriting or unfaithful relay on the data plane, undermining LLM routing integrity. We present VeriRouter, a verifiable LLM routing framework. Under an endorsed public context binding a private semantic index and rewrite banks, VeriRouter combines ZK proofs with a provider-issued serving certificate to establish integrity across both planes while keeping the router's private routing assets hidden from clients. For model selection, we design an efficient ZK proof for semantic search. For rewriting, local checks enforce message preservation and additions from committed banks. On real-world workloads, VeriRouter's model-selection and rewrite proofs average 21.92~s and 4.24~s, yielding 1,307$\times$ and 101$\times$ speedups over the fastest completing baselines. Relative to serving without verification, VeriRouter adds only 4.08 s under per-turn selection and 0.11 s under session-pinned selection.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
Security & Program Analysis.summary: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node.js 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node.js 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Penumbra: Sample-Efficient Adversarial Search for Regulatory Obligations
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agents are entering finance, healthcare and law, sectors where a violation leaves no lexical signature and carries real penalties. Whether an omission is material, or a disclosure sufficient, depends on what the response left out. Probing such an obligation means finding responses one minimal edit from flipping compliance, and every probe costs a generation and two adjudications, so the binding constraint on regulatory red-teaming is sample efficiency, not volume. We introduce Penumbra, an adversarial search that walks from a verified anchor under an expanding edit budget until a two-evaluator committee changes its verdict, and emits the two adjacent responses that straddle the change. Allocation is adaptive, and the objective is coverage of the defeat surface: distinct (obligation x defeat mode) cells resolved per candidate. At matched budget, adaptive allocation reaches uniform allocation's full-budget coverage on 59% of the candidates; at equal records it covers 1.43x the defeat modes of naive enumeration, and the gain is confined to the axis it targets. On 60 screened obligations of a financial advisory constitution, Penumbra returns 144 pairs, each a compliant and a violating response that the committee places on opposite sides of the boundary, differing by a handful of words where a model asked for both directly produces texts sharing almost nothing. A second constitution, for clinical triage, reproduces this on 18 obligations: 49 pairs at the same tightness, with the same modes hardest. Pairs like these show where an obligation's own terms stop deciding, which is what an agent deployed under it must be tested against, and the search finds them at a cost that scales with the boundary, not the text.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust) at NeurIPS 2026. Workshop papers are non-archival. 12 pages (4 content pages plus references and appendices)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

Security & Program Analysis.title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.

Security & Program Analysis.title: How Benchmarks and Evaluation Protocols Shape Conclusions in Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Provenance-based intrusion detection systems (PIDS) frequently report strong performance, but the conclusions drawn from these results can be highly sensitive to benchmarking choices and evaluation protocols. We investigate this dependency by re-evaluating representative PIDS on public datasets that meet our audit, labeling, and calibration requirements. Focusing primarily on the audited DARPA TC E3 datasets, we apply a unified protocol with temporally separated test periods and validation-only checkpoint selection and threshold calibration, and ask which architectural claims are empirically supported. We find that alerting success and investigation utility can diverge sharply, as several systems surface attacks without providing enough process-level context to support forensic investigation. Across the four primary datasets, a simple allowlist built from executable names and paths observed during training matches or exceeds the selected learned baselines on key operating-point metrics, showing that comparable performance on these metrics is achievable using lexical novelty alone. Quantifying semantic signal quality through feature completeness and field entropy helps explain why several audited E3 datasets support alerting performance without reliably separating model architectures. Theia, however, provides the richest semantic signal and is the only primary dataset on which our reference model, Theseus, clearly improves both ranking and node-level recovery over the other learned systems. Overall, these findings reinforce the importance of interpreting architectural claims in PIDS together with the benchmark properties and evaluation protocol that produced them.

Security & Program Analysis.title: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positions. Across LLaVA v1.5-7B, MiniGPT-4, and HuluMed-32B, spanning pretraining, instruction-tuning, and medical-image datasets, COMPASS outperforms baselines. On general-domain data, COMPASS achieves AUCs up to 0.88. On the distribution-matched medical evaluation, it reaches 0.64 AUC, while the strongest baseline remains at chance level. These results establish full-range adaptive perturbation analysis as an effective approach to VLLM membership inference.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SSM-Attack: Learning Where to Perturb for Black-Box Face Privacy
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Face recognition systems are deployed widely enough that a photograph shared online can be matched without its subject's consent. Generator-based protection methods rely on heavy pretrained backbones, multi-stage inference or visible semantic edits. We introduce SSM-Attack, a black-box face privacy framework built on Selective State Space Models. Rather than synthesizing the perturbation, the state-space model predicts in one linear-time pass a spatial allocation of the perturbation budget, marking which facial locations carry identity evidence; a short projected refinement then sets the values within this per-pixel budget. Against published benchmark results, SSM-Attack attains the highest average black-box attack success rate on all three evaluation sets: 87.10 percent on CelebA-HQ, 86.90 on LADN and 81.15 on FFHQ, the last from a network that never saw that dataset. The allocation network holds 5.73 million parameters, or 16.13 million with the frozen networks used by its quality terms. Under the same cap of 0.10 on the maximum per-pixel change, allocation improves structural similarity by 0.044, peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 decibels and Frechet Inception Distance by 11.2 points over a uniform map while spending 37 percent of its capacity. Strong facial privacy protection therefore does not require a large generative prior; it requires knowing where to spend a small one.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 25 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Preprint submitted to Pattern Recognition

Security & Program Analysis.title: NeuroFilter: Activation-Based Guardrails for Privacy-Conscious LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) are models able to reason, plan, and execute tools over unstructured data. These abilities enable transformative applications in domains spanning personal assistants, financial, and legal domains, etc. While these systems can substantially improve productivity and service quality, effective agency typically requires access to sensitive personal or organizational information. However, this access introduces critical inference-time privacy risks, specifically regarding contextually appropriate information disclosure. While recent studies highlight the inability of agentic LLMs to consistently adhere to privacy norms, existing defenses often rely on auxiliary LLM-based monitors. However, these defenses are expensive and offer limited protection against attacks that are robust to semantic censorship. To contrast this background, this paper proposes a notion of privacy filters based on activation probing. We show that these filters are both computationally efficient and effective for both single-turn and multi-turn conversational settings. Furthermore, this work provides the first systematic investigation into probing model internals across a conversation trajectory, moving beyond static, single-prompt analysis to capture the evolving state of privacy-sensitive interactions, illustrating their applicability across contexts, attack styles, multiple base models, and challenging settings such as mosaic attacks, while providing nuanced insights into the nature of the discovered concepts and modular construction of probes.

Security & Program Analysis.title: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned LLMs show that TRAP outperforms its counterparts on six models under the reported method settings and the common primary evaluator, achieving attack success rates of 45.6% to 97.9% on these models. These findings support hierarchical strategy learning as an effective approach to discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Tight End-to-End Accounting for Differentially Private Synthetic Data
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Differentially private (DP) pipelines often combine heterogeneous mechanisms, yet their guarantees are best analyzed using different notions of privacy (e.g., bounded range, zCDP, ADP). When composing them, we have to analyze the guarantees through a reduced common representation that loses accounting precision. This issue is particularly relevant in DP synthetic data generation, where data preprocessing, generation algorithms, and DP-SGD could appear within the same pipeline. We develop novel tools for tight end-to-end accounting of such compositions using privacy loss distributions (PLD), $f$-DP, and Gaussian DP (GDP). In particular, we derive PLD and GDP analyses of bounded-range mechanisms such as the Exponential mechanism. Building on these theoretical results, we introduce AIM-GDP, a GDP-native variant of AIM (a state-of-the-art DP synthetic data mechanism) that enables easy composability with complex pipelines via PLD, attack-aware risk calibration, and tight end-to-end auditing while consistently achieving better utility; and MixCal, an algorithm for calibrating adaptive mixed compositions using PLD accounting. Overall, our tools enable tighter end-to-end accounting and thus less noise at the same privacy level in DP synthetic data pipelines.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Dependency-Aware Privacy for Multi-turn LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
LLM agents release private data across multi-service interactions. Existing prompt sanitizers based on metric differential privacy treat each release independently, so adversaries combining releases across turns can recover private attributes; privacy degrades with every release.
  This degradation is fundamental: when private attributes are the \emph{roots} of a computation graph, independently noising a derived value amplifies the root's distinguishability by up to the deriving function's Lipschitz constant $L$, which can far exceed the nominal privacy parameter for nonlinear functions in medical and financial workflows.
  RootGuard sanitizes root values once and computes subsequent releases deterministically from the noised roots. By the post-processing theorem, the privacy guarantee depends only on the initial root sanitization, regardless of the adversary's functions or number of turns, and derived values inherit privacy at zero marginal cost. RootGuard further exploits structural domain knowledge (e.g., BMI from height and weight, or a known target function) to allocate budget across roots, improving the privacy-utility tradeoff.
  A worst-case adversary forcing $t$ turns increases the total budget $B = t \cdot \varepsilon$. RootGuard distributes this larger budget across roots, while independent noising spends $\varepsilon$ per release and gives the adversary $t$ observations to combine via MAP reconstruction. This yields a \emph{double asymmetry}: more turns aid RootGuard while weakening independent noising.
  On eight NHANES medical diagnostic templates, RootGuard achieves $2.6\times$ lower target error than independent noising at $\varepsilon = 0.1$ (7.8\% vs.\ 20.3\% wMAPE at $B = (2k{+}1)\varepsilon$). Under MAP reconstruction, more queries strengthen attacks against independent noising while RootGuard remains invariant.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Exploring Vulnerabilities and Concerns in Solana Smart Contracts
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The Solana blockchain was created by Anatoly Yakovenko of Solana Labs and was introduced in 2017, employing a novel transaction verification method. However, at the same time, the innovation process introduced some new security issues. The frequent security incidents in smart contracts have not only caused enormous economic losses, but also undermined the credit system based on the blockchain. The security and reliability of smart contracts have become a new focus of research both domestically and abroad. This paper studies the current status of security analysis of Solana by researching Solana smart contract security analysis tools. This paper systematically sorts out the vulnerabilities existing in Solana smart contracts and gives examples of some vulnerabilities, summarizes the principles of security analysis tools, and comprehensively summarizes and details the security analysis tools in Solana smart contracts. The data of Solana smart contract security analysis tools are collected and compared with Ethereum, and the differences are analyzed and some tools are selected for practical testing.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SEAL-DT: An End-to-End Security Engineering and Assurance Framework for Cross-Domain Digital Twins
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cyber-physical systems connect physical processes, software, networks and organizations. Securing them requires a clear account of what happened, what was observed, which actions were authorized and what evidence supports each decision. Digital Twin (DT) descriptions often fail to explain how these elements stay consistent, blur the distinction between physical events and uncertain observations, or detach simulation results from their requirements and assumptions. This paper presents SEAL-DT (Security Engineering and Assurance Lifecycle for Digital Twins), a structured approach to building and evaluating secure DTs. It brings entity definitions, process models, deterministic simulations, data contracts, evidence records, automated tests and reproducible results into one connected model. The main contribution is an end-to-end DT security framework, spanning scenario definition, entity/process modelling, simulation, security decision logic, evidence handling, validation and reproducible reporting. Security decisions and simulation results thus trace back to their data, assumptions and requirements. A DT is more than a copy of system state: it states what it can observe, how accurate and current its information is, where it came from and which decisions it may support. We demonstrate SEAL-DT in five scenarios: Car2X protection, passive IoT-device detection, an industrial control surrogate, lawful acquisition in a smart home, and medical-IoT monitoring that preserves continuity of care. Each includes formal models, deterministic and negative experiments, uncertainty analyses, schema-valid fixtures, technical reports and verified manifests, testing multiple configurations under normal and adverse conditions. Results show that the framework supports consistent model construction, traceable execution and comparable internal validation, and that security findings link to observable evidence.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Penetration Testing for System Security: Methods and Practical Approaches
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Penetration testing refers to the process of simulating hacker attacks to evaluate the security of information systems . This study aims not only to clarify the theoretical foundations of penetration testing but also to explain and demonstrate the complete testing process, including how network system administrators may simulate attacks using various penetration testing methods. Methodologically, the paper outlines the five basic stages of a typical penetration test: intelligence gathering, vulnerability scanning, vulnerability exploitation, privilege escalation, and post-exploitation activities. In each phase, specific tools and techniques are examined in detail, along with practical guidance on their use. To enhance the practical relevance of the study, the paper also presents a real-life case study, illustrating how a complete penetration test is conducted in a real-world environment. Through this case, readers can gain insights into the detailed procedures and applied techniques, thereby deepening their understanding of the practical value of penetration testing. Finally, the paper summarizes the importance and necessity of penetration testing in securing information systems and maintaining network integrity, and it explores future trends and development directions for the field. Overall, the findings of this paper offer valuable references for both researchers and practitioners, contributing meaningfully to the improvement of penetration testing practices and the advancement of cybersecurity as a whole.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted for publication in IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (TCHES)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Preserving Structure, Strengthening Signals: A Grammar-Driven Approach to Optimize the Trade-off Between Quality and Detectability in Code Watermarking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Text watermarking has emerged as a crucial technique for identifying AI-generated content. However, current watermarking schemes entail a trade-off between text quality and watermark detectability, which is further intensified by the inherent low-entropy nature of code. To mitigate this dilemma, we propose Grammar-Driven Watermark (GDW), a training-free watermarking approach tailored to LLM-based code generation. GDW employs a three-level masking mechanism consisting of a green-list mask, a syntactic validity mask, and a structural role mask to regulate watermark injection. These masks are integrated through hierarchical modulation, which limits the scope of watermark injection to syntactically admissible green-list tokens and adjusts watermark strength based on structural roles through a role function. Accordingly, we design a role-aware weighted detection statistic. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce the Area Under the Trade-off Curve (AUTC), a metric that quantifies the quality-detectability trade-off. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GDW outperforms existing baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) trade-off performance, while maintaining superior performance under seven semantics-preserving attacks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ZIMPAF & RedPhuzz: High-fidelity Web Application Fuzzing via Branch, Language Construct, and Function Call Monitoring
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We present ZIMPAF, runtime interpreter instrumentation, and RedPhuzz, a fuzzer, to realize high-fidelity fuzzing framework. ZIMPAF implements multi-granular interceptors to collect traces of branch coverage, errors and exceptions, functions and language constructs, and input-tainted branches. It identifies tainted vulnerable functions, marking them as high-value fuzzing targets, and untainted vulnerable functions using in-situ static analysis called backward constant probe, allowing them to be skipped, without pre-fuzzing static taint analysis. The traces are utilized by RedPhuzz to perform targeted function- and input-level fuzzing that goes beyond traditional coverage-based fuzzing, supported by three novel mutation strategies: sanitization-aware, input-in-branch-aware, and data-type-aware mutation. Furthermore, we introduce multi-stage vulnerability detection that extends beyond error- and exception-based detection, capable of detecting silent vulnerabilities. We evaluate RedPhuzz's performance against its predecessor, Phuzz, on 86 test cases across six benchmark web applications. RedPhuzz detects all vulnerabilities, whereas Phuzz fails to detect 16. RedPhuzz is 77% faster than Phuzz despite performing more tasks. ZIMPAF is faster than Phuzz's instrumentation (PCOV and UOPZ) while writing significantly more data. ZIMPAF achieves 2.1 to 41.22 times higher throughput than PCOV and UOPZ across five sampled benchmarks, and 0.87 times for one.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The shifted-prime Erdős-Wintner law for primitive-root determinant densities: extremal order, dimension zero, and Fourier decay
Security & Program Analysis.summary: For a prime $p$, let $c(p)=\frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\prod_{j\ge1}(1-p^{-j})$, the limiting density of matrices over $\mathbb F_p$ with primitive-root determinant. Its limiting law over the primes is the classical continuous shifted-totient law on $[0,1/2]$. We prove that this law has Hausdorff dimension zero and is carried by the Liouville numbers; its lower and upper dyadic $L^q$ dimensions vanish for $q>1$. Its logarithmic image $μ_f$ under $x\mapsto-\log x$ is Rajchman and satisfies $|\widehat{μ_f}(τ)|\ll(\log|τ|)^{-1/3}(\log\log|τ|)^{1/3}$ with effective constants and threshold. For $U_T$ uniform on $[0,T]$, $(\log T)|\widehat{μ_f}(U_T)|$ converges in law to an explicit random Euler product $W_F$, and $T^{-1}\int_0^T|\widehat{μ_f}(τ)|^s dτ\sim\mathbb E[W_F^s]/(\log T)^s$ for every fixed real $s>-1$. As $h\downarrow0$, $\sup_aμ_f([a,a+h])=\mathfrak S_2e^{-γ}/\log(1/h)+O(\log^{-2}(1/h))$, where $\mathfrak S_2$ is the twin-prime singular series; every maximizing left endpoint lies within $h$ of $\log3$ for small $h$. Classical arguments give $\min_{p\le x}c(p)\sim e^{-γ}/\log\log x$; we obtain effective additive remainders and extrema in fixed reduced progressions. The laws of $σ(p-1)/(p-1)$ on $[3/2,\infty)$ and $\log(\varphi(p+1)/\varphi(p-1))$ on $\mathbb R$ also have Hausdorff dimension zero; the logarithmic divisor-sum law is Rajchman. Rational bounds for $1/c(p)$ without complete factorization of $p-1$ yield certified searches for fully splitting negacyclic number-theoretic transform primes at fixed power-of-two length. We determine the second distinct squared norm of tensor products of root lattices $A_n$ ($n\ge1$), yielding cyclotomic codifferent shell gaps and a uniform smoothing asymptotic at $ε=2^{-c\varphi(m)}$ for $c>2\log_2(1+\sqrt6)$. These results are unconditional.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Substantially revised: unconditional effective Fourier decay replaces the previous conditional quantitative estimate; added Fourier-amplitude limit laws, Liouville and normality results, and strengthened arithmetic and smoothing estimates. Exposition and references updated

Security & Program Analysis.title: Security and robustness analysis of encrypted communications for local home automation: ESPHome Native API and MQTT over TLS 1.3
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in residential and local automation environments has highlighted the limitations of considering the internal network as an inherently trusted domain. Man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, such as ARP spoofing, can allow traffic interception or manipulation when communications lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, and authentication mechanisms. This paper presents a systematized review of the security mechanisms used by two communication alternatives between ESP-family microcontrollers and the Home Assistant platform: MQTT protected through TLS 1.3 and the ESPHome Native API, whose encryption is based on the Noise Protocol Framework using the Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 pattern. The analysis considers four dimensions: cryptographic robustness, attack surface, implementation complexity, and resource consumption. The review identifies significant differences resulting from the architecture and cryptographic model of each alternative. TLS 1.3 provides a standardized framework compatible with public-key infrastructure and formal identity management, though it introduces greater configuration complexity and computational overhead during session establishment. The ESPHome Native API employs a more specialized scheme with lower operational complexity, eliminates dynamic algorithm negotiation, and uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. The resource-consumption analysis relies on measurements published by the projects and manufacturers themselves, not on an experimental test bench, and this limitation is explicitly acknowledged. The results identify the conditions under which each mechanism is appropriate for local home-automation architectures and provide a basis for designing IoT systems that balance security, interoperability, and resource constraints.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Systematized review. Submitted to the International Journal of Network Security & Its Applications (IJNSA)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Scrambled Linear Pseudorandom Number Generators
Security & Program Analysis.summary: $\mathbf F_2$-linear pseudorandom number generators are very popular due to their high speed, to the ease with which generators with a sizable state space can be created, and to their provable theoretical properties. However, they suffer from linear artifacts that show as failures in linearity-related statistical tests such as the binary-rank and the linear-complexity test. In this paper, we give two new contributions. First, we introduce two new $\mathbf F_2$-linear transformations that have been handcrafted to have good statistical properties and at the same time to be programmable very efficiently on superscalar processors, or even directly in hardware. Then, we describe some scramblers, that is, nonlinear functions applied to the state array that reduce or delete the linear artifacts, and propose combinations of linear transformations and scramblers that give extremely fast pseudorandom number generators of high quality. A novelty in our approach is that we use ideas from the theory of filtered linear-feedback shift registers to prove some properties of our scramblers, rather than relying purely on heuristics. In the end, we provide simple, extremely fast generators that use a few hundred bits of memory, have provable properties, and pass strong statistical tests.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Survey of Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge, but this access path creates security risks distinct from inherent prompt-only or parametric-model flaws. We frame secure RAG as securing external knowledge access. We conducted a systematic search and curated 135 works on attacks, defenses, and security evaluation, and organized them with SLOT: a taxonomy along the attack Surface (S) and the corresponding defense Layer (L), with cross-cutting axes Objective (O) and attack-target scope (T). Mapping these studies onto an external knowledge-access pipeline, we expose three mismatches: target mismatch (T2 attacks outpace T2 defenses and evaluation), stage mismatch (S1 attacks outnumber L1 defenses), and signal mismatch (fluent, retrievable, corpus-fitting S1 attacks challenge anomaly-based L2/L3 defenses). Finally, we discuss directions for more realistic targets, surface-complete defense stacks, standardized evaluation, confidentiality, and multimodal and agentic systems, and release the screening process, selected-paper metadata, and machine-readable SLOT labels at https://github.com/TreeAI-Lab/Awesome-RAG-Security.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Illusion of Local Privacy: Confidentiality Boundary Failures in Consumer LLM Serving Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Running large language models (LLMs) locally is often considered more private than cloud-hosted inference because user prompts remain on the device. We ask whether keeping inference local is, by itself, sufficient to keep those prompts confidential. Our results show that it is not: prompt confidentiality also depends on how the surrounding serving software handles prompt data before, during, and after inference. We examine four boundaries at which prompt confidentiality can fail in consumer local-LLM serving systems: model loading, runtime memory, wrapper-level persistence, and the serving interface. To study these boundaries, we develop LLAnalyzer, a measurement framework that tests each boundary separately and traces observed failures to the responsible software component. Applying LLAnalyzer to four open-weight model families and two consumer deployment platforms, we find markedly different behaviour across boundaries. In a 24-hour AFL++ campaign with more than 12 million executions, we observe no parser crashes or successful malformed GGUF loads within the explored state space. Runtime memory tells a different story: we recover prompts after inference because multiple plaintext representations survive in allocator-managed memory, and sanitisation reduces this residue without eliminating it. We also find that consumer wrappers can extend prompt lifetime through plaintext persistence. At the serving boundary, we uncover a previously undocumented authorization flaw in llama.cpp that allows one authenticated client to restore another tenant's saved conversation state; the attack succeeds in 200/200 controlled trials. Separately, shared prompt-prefix caching exposes a remote timing oracle that remains distinguishable under WAN conditions. We argue that local LLM systems need explicit guarantees for prompt lifetime, persistent storage, and tenant isolation.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 16 pages, 2 figure, 12 tables. Code and experimental artifacts: https://github.com/0xzodiac/Local-LLMs-Forensics, Preprint for IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (T-IFS)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Risk Assessment and Security Analysis of Large Language Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As large language models (LLMs) expose systemic security challenges in high risk applications, including privacy leaks, bias amplification, and malicious abuse, there is an urgent need for a dynamic risk assessment and collaborative defence framework that covers their entire life cycle. This paper focuses on the security problems of large language models (LLMs) in critical application scenarios, such as the possibility of disclosure of user data, the deliberate input of harmful instructions, or the models bias. To solve these problems, we describe the design of a system for dynamic risk assessment and a hierarchical defence system that allows different levels of protection to cooperate. This paper presents a risk assessment system capable of evaluating both static and dynamic indicators simultaneously. It uses entropy weighting to calculate essential data, such as the frequency of sensitive words, whether the API call is typical, the realtime risk entropy value is significant, and the degree of context deviation. The experimental results show that the system is capable of identifying concealed attacks, such as role escape, and can perform rapid risk evaluation. The paper uses a hybrid model called BERT-CRF (Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers) at the input layer to identify and filter malicious commands. The model layer uses dynamic adversarial training and differential privacy noise injection technology together. The output layer also has a neural watermarking system that can track the source of the content. In practice, the quality of this method, especially important in terms of customer service in the financial industry.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Fast Abstract presented at IEEE QRS 2026 (Florence, Italy)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Blockchain security based on cryptography: a review
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As an emerging service framework built by combining cryptography, P2P network, consensus mechanism and innovative contract technology, blockchain has been widely used in digital finance, data sharing, message traceability and electronic evidence preservation because of its decentralised, non-tamperable and transaction traceability. However, with the complex and changeable application scenarios of blockchain technology and the continuous enhancement of blockchain attack technology, the security of the blockchain system has been seriously threatened, dramatically affecting the development and application of blockchain technology. This paper aims to analyse the attacks on blockchain from the perspective of cryptography. Firstly, from the cryptography technology in the blockchain, the principle of hash functions, digital signatures, and other technologies, as well as their role in the blockchain, are introduced. Then, based on the six-layer architecture of the blockchain, the attacks on the data layer, the network layer, the consensus layer, the contract layer, the incentive layer and the application layer are analysed, and the methods to mitigate or resist the attacks are proposed. Secondly, the attack principles of 51% attack, Double-Spending attack, Reentrancy attack, Replay attack, Sybil attack and Timestamp Tampering attack were analysed, and the mitigation or defence solutions for these six attacks were designed. Finally, the core problems to be solved in blockchain technology are summarised, and the future development of blockchain security technology is projected.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Deepfake speech detectors are typically evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions, with labels unavailable during operation. This makes it difficult to know when a detector operates in familiar conditions and can be relied on. We propose an unsupervised drift monitor that operates on the internal embeddings of a deployed detector. The monitor compares each input against bona fide and spoof references using regularized Mahalanobis distances. These distances define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the detector embedding space, allowing unfamiliar inputs to be routed for review. We evaluate the monitor on four modern detectors on three datasets. The monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage. The results also show that drift affects both classes: bona fide recordings can move away from the training reference, increasing alert rates even in in-domain settings. Our findings suggest that deployed deepfake speech detectors should be treated not only as a binary classification, but also as a reliability problem.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at IEEE International Workshop on Information Forensics and Security (WIFS) 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.

Security & Program Analysis.title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: From Chasing Ghosts to Missed Attacks: Perspectives and Perceptions of SOC Practitioners on LLM Integration, Risks, and Readiness
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) process large volumes of security events, requiring analysts to accurately detect and assess ongoing cyberattacks under time pressure. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) suggest potential benefits for security operations, yet their practical suitability for real-world SOC workflows remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners who had prior experience with LLMs, complemented by interactive scenarios to anticipate challenges and identify opportunities for the responsible integration of LLM-based tools into SOC workflows. We identified 15 LLM use cases grouped into six functional categories. While LLMs are valued for automating repetitive, low-level tasks such as report automation, practitioners rate high-impact tasks such as incident analysis as not yet feasible, reporting limitations in technical depth, context awareness, and organization-specific knowledge. They locate these limitations less in the models than in the readiness of their SOCs and human factors driving over-reliance. Despite concerns, practitioners express a strong willingness to adopt LLMs, describing competitive pressure that leaves few alternatives. This work contributes an empirical, practitioner-driven analysis of LLM use across SOC roles and organizations and derives concrete design and integration requirements for human-centered, operationally safe LLM-assisted security operations.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Comparative Analysis of Blockchain Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Blockchain is a type of decentralized distributed database. Unlike traditional relational database management systems, it does not require management or maintenance by a third party. All data management and update processes are open and transparent, solving the trust issues of centralized database management systems. Blockchain ensures network-wide consistency, consensus, traceability, and immutability. Under the premise of mutual distrust between nodes, blockchain technology integrates various technologies, such as P2P protocols, asymmetric encryption, consensus mechanisms, and chain structures. Data is distributed and stored across multiple nodes, maintained by all nodes, ensuring transaction data integrity, undeniability, and security. This facilitates trusted information sharing and supervision. The basic principles of blockchain form the foundation for all related research. Understanding the working principles is essential for further study of blockchain technology. There are many platforms based on blockchain technology, and they differ from one another. This paper will analyze the architecture of blockchain systems at each layer, focusing on the principles and technologies of blockchain platforms such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Hyperledger Fabric. The analysis will cover their scalability and security and highlight their similarities, differences, advantages, and disadvantages.

Security & Program Analysis.title: CT0: Cybersecurity Transformer
Security & Program Analysis.summary: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for the facts it is unsure about, extracts vulnerability facts more accurately than either mode alone at a fifth of the generative cost. All of it is built in about 314 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours and served from one workstation GPU, with no policy layer between operator and target. Across eighteen benchmarks and use cases run with one checkpoint and head, we report where the design helps, where it does not, and what it still lacks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: CircuitBreak: Pruning a Sparse Safety Circuit of Neurons
Security & Program Analysis.summary: White-box neuron pruning has shown that refusal in large language models (LLMs) can depend on a small, removable set of feed-forward (FFN) channels. Existing attacks either need carefully paired ``twin'' prompts or score each neuron in isolation. Pruning also has an unavoidable capability cost, so over-removal compounds the loss. TwinBreak removes $1\%$--$5\%$ of parameters and NeuroStrike removes $0.3\%$--$0.7\%$ of neurons in targeted layers. We model safety as a small \emph{circuit} whose neurons contribute jointly rather than independently. We propose \textsc{CircuitBreak}, a neuron-pruning attack that greedily searches for a sparse set of FFN neurons whose joint ablation flips a refusal readout. \textsc{CircuitBreak} re-scores every candidate after the neurons already removed and needs no twin prompts. On ten instruction-tuned models, the greedy search converges after removing $29$--$150$ neurons ($0.0066\%$--$0.0388\%$ of the MLP). The pruned models raise the attack success rate from $2.24\%$/$7.35\%$ to $87.54\%$/$87.54\%$ on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from $8.95\%$/$5.43\%$ to $88.50\%$/$88.18\%$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, as judged by Llama Guard 3 8B on StrongREJECT.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.

Security & Program Analysis.title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Divide, Consult, Conquer: Capability Laundering Through Aligned LLMs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Language model safety is typically evaluated one interaction at a time. We show that a weaker, unaligned model can split a harmful task into benign-looking subproblems, consult a stronger aligned model independently on each, and combine the answers locally. We call this attack capability laundering. Unlike a jailbreak, no single response is a harmful task. We measure consultation-aided uplift using tasks that a raw frontier model solves, the aligned frontier refuses, and the unassisted orchestrator fails. We evaluate GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Grok-4.3 as consultants to four local orchestrators on CyBench, BountyBench, and harmful CBRN requests. On CyBench, Gemma-4-31B recovers 8/14 candidates with GPT-5.5 and 7/9 with Opus, compared with 2/21 and 4/15 for Gemma-4-12B. On BountyBench, Gemma-4-31B recovers 3/9 and 2/3 candidates, while Muse-Glimmer-30B recovers none of 22 and 13. For CBRN, we measure uplift across eight steps of a hypothetical bioweapon attack chain and find that consultation raises Gemma-4-31B's mean rubric score from 62.3 to 83.1 on a 100-point rubric scale. These results expose a gap in current defenses: refusing a harmful task does not prevent frontier capabilities from being transferred and composed across many individually permitted interactions.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Revisiting Fast Tendermint: An Agreement Violation and Two Repairs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Fast Tendermint reduces Tendermint's good-case latency to two communication steps for n>=5f+1. We show that its published round-change rule violates Agreement: one Byzantine process suffices for every f>=1, and for f>=2 two Byzantine processes suffice without double signing. The failure occurs when a process advances past a round without recording the value that may have been decided there. The Quint specification that accompanies the protocol does not allow this kind of round skipping and is not affected; the violation lies in the published pseudocode. We present two repairs. Walk requires a process to leave each round on a quorum of that round's precommits and to precommit before leaving. It keeps the recorded valid state and removes the wait after a precommit quorum.
