Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: In-Context Learning Before Specialisation: Theory of Learning in a Solvable Topic Model
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Sequence models can generalise in fundamentally distinct ways: extrapolating structures seen in training, or using their prompt to adapt to novel tasks. The prevailing strategy determines how the model behaves beyond its training distribution, controlling potential capabilities and risks. Recent work has characterised many different strategies theoretically, and empirically described the transition between them as the quality and quantity of pretraining data vary. However, there is no learning theory for this competition, hence no fundamental understanding of \textit{why} one solution might be favoured over another. Here we provide such a theory in a solvable topic model---documents drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data. The dataset comes with two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor, that stores the finite topic mixture, and an in-context one, optimal for topics never seen during training. Our theory predicts their emergence at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor is available early, while the specialised one emerges only after the training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the separating crossover in remarkable agreement with the theory, with no fitted parameters.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Provably Efficient Risk-Sensitive Offline Reinforcement Learning via Optimized Certainty Equivalents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: JEPA-DNA: Grounding Genomic Foundation Models through Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) typically rely on Masked Language Modeling (MLM) or Next-Token Prediction (NTP) to learn the "Laws of Nature". While effective at capturing local syntax, these generative paradigms prioritize token-level reconstruction over high-level functional context. We introduce JEPA-DNA, a model-agnostic continual training framework that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) with traditional generative objectives. By supervising global sequence embeddings in a latent space, JEPA-DNA forces models to predict the functional representations of masked genomic segments, shifting the learning signal from token recovery to semantic alignment. We evaluate JEPA-DNA on 17 diverse genomic benchmark tasks, demonstrating consistent gains in linear probing and zero-shot performance regardless of the underlying GFM architecture or generative objective, and establishing a new state-of-the-art for GFMs under the linear-probing protocol. Through extensive ablation studies, we further characterize the synergistic interplay between generative and latent objectives. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Words Speak Louder Than Code: Investigating Cognitive Heuristics in LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Researchers and practitioners increasingly apply Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated vulnerability detection. Recent work has shown that LLMs are susceptible to the same cognitive heuristics that bias human judgment. Yet, no work has investigated whether these heuristics affect a model's assessment of code vulnerabilities. In this paper, we present the first systematic exploration of cognitive heuristics in LLM-driven code vulnerability detection. We introduce a controlled framework that holds the code fixed and only varies the surrounding context to trigger three cognitive heuristics: the halo effect through author attribution, the framing effect through task objectives and consequences, and the anchoring effect through prior analysis results. Within this framework, we evaluate eight LLMs across three programming languages. Our results demonstrate that all evaluated models are susceptible to these heuristics. Cross-model average susceptibility is highest for framing at 33.2%, followed by anchoring at 23.5% and halo at 18.4%. Vulnerabilities that require semantic reasoning for detection are more susceptible to cognitive heuristics than those identifiable through pattern matching. Furthermore, models often change their verdict from safe to vulnerable based on the cognitive condition, without accurately identifying the actual vulnerability. To highlight the practical impact, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept black-box cognitive attack that can suppress up to 97\% of previously detected vulnerabilities. Together, these findings show that cognitive bias is a consistent and exploitable property of LLM-based vulnerability detection.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Accepted at IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (IEEE S&P) 2027

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: E$^2$-OPSD: Taming Entropy Overshoot in On-Policy Self-Distillation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense token-level supervision without a second model: one network acts as teacher with the reference solution and as student with only the problem. We identify a specific failure mode of this recipe. During training, student token entropy rises past the teacher's and remains elevated, a pattern we call entropy overshoot. We trace it to both sides of distillation. The reference-conditioned teacher is confident along its answer-directed reasoning path, but this confidence transfers poorly to student-generated prefixes, making its supervision overly tied to answer-specific cues rather than reusable reasoning patterns; meanwhile, the forward KL used by OPSD continually diffuses the student's predictive distribution without pulling it back. We introduce E$^2$-OPSD to address both causes. Exemplar-guided teaching replaces the current answer with a retrieved solved neighboring problem, providing transferable reasoning guidance without revealing the destination and better matching student-reachable states. Entropy-aware distillation uses the student-teacher entropy gap to determine the direction and strength of each token's correction. E$^2$-OPSD improves math reasoning by up to 4.3 points in mean@16 over OPSD, while out-of-domain evaluations show gains over the corresponding base models of up to 4.9 points in mean@16 and 5.5 points in pass@8. Despite these gains, E$^2$-OPSD remains simple, requiring no additional forward passes or networks. Code repo: https://github.com/orionfei/E2-OPSD.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CIM-Embed: Learning Instruction-Conditioned Multimodal Embeddings for Clustering
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Multimodal objects can require different partitions under different instructions, as when products in an e-commerce catalog are grouped by color, material, or both. Retrieval-oriented embeddings may not recover these partitions, while generative clustering often relies on intermediate descriptions or iterative decisions. This paper presents CIM-Embed, a framework for learning instruction-conditioned multimodal embeddings for clustering. Supervised contrastive learning uses same-group positives and negatives from other groups, optionally including other tasks; heterogeneous structured batches accommodate tasks with different group counts. At inference, the model maps each object's image, text, and instruction directly to an embedding; HDBSCAN then forms a partition without the ground-truth cluster count. We construct ProductMIC from product metadata in Amazon Reviews 2023, comprising training data and an evaluation benchmark for instruction-conditioned clustering. The benchmark contains 5,373 products and 449 single-attribute and compositional grouping tasks spanning 50 leaf categories excluded from our training. With full-dimensional embeddings and HDBSCAN, direct within-task SupCon training achieves a mean per-task V-measure of 95.01, compared with 53.06 for WeMM 9B, the strongest general-purpose embedding baseline evaluated. Frozen product-trained encoders also improve out-of-domain conditional grouping, while controlled transfer experiments distinguish partition transfer from instruction response. We will release the code and dataset upon acceptance.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Incremental learning (IL) aims to continually acquire new knowledge (plasticity) while retaining previously learned information (stability). However, striking a balance between plasticity and stability remains a significant challenge for intelligent systems. The human brain achieves exceptional balance, owing to various memory units that collaboratively encode and store information. Inspired by human memory mechanisms, this paper introduces an IL framework with knowledge enCoding, Consolidation, and Integration (Co2In). Co2In is designed as a bi-level memory architecture: a working memory for adaptive knowledge acquisition and a long-term memory dedicated to the persistent retention of information. The two memory modules work cooperatively during IL. The working memory first learns from new data to encode knowledge into parameters. Subsequently, Co2In performs a consolidation process to identify underlying patterns in the learned parameters and re-express them into a compact knowledge representation. Next, the knowledge representation and the identified patterns are transformed into separate network layers and integrated into the long-term memory. These designs empower Co2In to accumulate knowledge with high plasticity and stability. We evaluate Co2In on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings. Experimental results show that Co2In achieves state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions On Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Agent Skill Framework: Perspectives on the Potential of Small to Medium Language Models in Industrial Environments
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Skills are getting increasingly used in recent agentic frameworks, performing robustly with proprietary LLMs. Yet, their effectiveness for small and medium-sized open-source models (270M--80B) remains underexplored, especially under industrial, resource-constrained conditions. As such, we present a large-scale empirical study evaluating the skill paradigm's feasibility across two open-source classification tasks: one insurance-claim task based on proprietary data, and a set of Python programming problems. We find that very small models frequently fail to retrieve or select correct skills, substantially limiting their usefulness in the evaluated skill-augmented settings, while larger 30B--80B models gain substantial benefits from skill augmentation. Furthermore, we provide a deployment-oriented GPU profile, reporting VRAM time occupancy (GB$\cdot$min) across models under our evaluation settings---a deployment-oriented metric that may help characterize GPU-memory costs, where small and medium models are typically preferred for VRAM control. These results characterize how the benefits of skill augmentation vary with model scale, task complexity, and GPU budget, and provide deployment-oriented observations.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: RefactorPlatform: An Open-Source Harness for Controlled Evaluation of Repository-Scale Refactoring Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Repository-scale refactoring requires coding agents to propagate a single change across many interdependent files without altering program behavior, yet to our knowledge no existing harness isolates the design choices that determine agent success on this task. We present RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that holds the environment fixed and varies each design axis explicitly: model backbone (via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI), execution regime (baseline, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent), and prompt specificity. Each run executes in an isolated workspace with live terminal streaming, per-task logging of tokens, diffs, and transcripts, AST-based verification, and exportable telemetry for audit and reproduction. Demonstrating the platform on 100 multi-file RefactorBench tasks across four model families, we illustrate the analyses it supports: AST-aware chunking outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30 percentage points (pp) across prompt modes, whereas naive retrieval falls below the retrieval-free baseline; a lean retrieval-augmented single agent (86%) beats the sub-agent configuration we evaluated (66%) on matched tasks with no task passing under delegation that fails under retrieval; and retrieval's accuracy gains absorb its token overhead, leaving cost per successful refactoring unchanged. RefactorPlatform is open-sourced to make refactoring-agent evaluation reproducible and auditable.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: In the Guise of Correction: How Framing and Cultural Adaptation Erode LLM Safety on Real-World Criminal Cases
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Existing safety benchmarks rely largely on synthetic prompts with loosely grounded taxonomies and offer little focused analysis of severe crime categories. We introduce GUISE, a benchmark of criminal-assistance scenarios sourced from real-world cases and organised under a taxonomy from the UNODC International Classification of Crime for Statistical Purposes (ICCS). Each scenario is rendered under three linguistic framings and evaluated across five distinct cultures. Using our proposed two-tier evaluation framework, which judges both harmfulness and operational uplift, we find that: (i) framing alone drives unsafe compliance, with the mean unsafe compliance rate rising from 28.9% under direct requests to 66.4% under correction seeking (peaking at 97.3%; p < 0.05), as models correcting deliberately distorted details supply executable criminal steps; (ii) culturally adapted prompts elicit significantly more unsafe compliance than literal translations of the same requests in all four non-English languages (+7 to +18 points), a risk that translation-based benchmarks miss; and (iii) unsafe responses from the least-safe models carry strong Anglocentric registers, and the extent of this leakage increases monotonically with response harmfulness ($ρ$ = 0.46 to 0.63 across languages, all p < 0.001). GUISE offers a grounded resource and fine-grained diagnostics for strengthening refusal alignment across languages and cultures. We publish our code and data to facilitate future research.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: DINO-FIL: Multi-Layer Transformer Fusion for Generative Inpainting Forgery Localization
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We propose DINO-FIL, a transformer-based framework for pixel-level localization of generative image forgeries. The method leverages multi-layer representations from a pretrained DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 encoder combined with a lightweight fusion decoder to capture both semantic structure and fine-grained texture inconsistencies introduced by image editing. By aggregating intermediate transformer features across depths, the model improves sensitivity to subtle, spatially localized artifacts that are often missed by standard single-layer approaches. We evaluate DINO-FIL in a cross-dataset setting, training on B-Free and testing on Beyond the Brush, CocoGlide, TGIF, and SAGI-D. The model achieves strong generalization, outperforming existing baselines on average and on four of five evaluated datasets, while maintaining a high true negative rate on pristine images.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design. Our code is available at https://github.com/MAX-7237/TOPS.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Don't Regenerate, Debug: A Domain-Specific Agent for Repairing Near-Miss Accelerator Kernels
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Kernel generation for hardware accelerators such as GPUs and NPUs has become a proving ground for large language models (LLMs), and state-of-the-art systems raise correctness through pipelines that couple LLMs with agentic reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. Such pipelines generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, discarding most of them and forgoing the opportunity to distill failures into reusable knowledge. Many discarded candidates are near-miss operators that compile and run but fail numerical validation; each embodies genuine domain knowledge and a nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. We argue for a paradigm shift: rather than regenerate, debug. Debugging is far more constrained than generating from scratch: the search space is small and feedback is dense. We present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three core challenges in autonomous repair: mitigating knowledge scarcity through retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Debugging serves two complementary roles: it extends the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and it lowers cost per deliverable operator. Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7% versus Regenerate Avg Pass@1's 25.9% and Regenerate Pass@3's 40.7%, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per success than three-trial regeneration. Component ablations show that the knowledge base drives recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5-33.3% of the successes the workflow itself accepted.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Efficiently Estimating Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Laws through Power-Law Entropy Search
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Optimal hyperparameter scaling laws describe how the best hyperparameters for large language model (LLM) training change with model and data scale, enabling practitioners to predict optimal configurations at production scales without expensive large-scale tuning. However, estimating these scaling laws conventionally requires exhaustive grid searches over thousands of training runs, consuming enormous computational resources. We introduce Power-Law Entropy Search (PLES), a computational cost-aware acquisition function built on multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization that efficiently estimates optimal hyperparameter scaling laws through adaptive experimentation. A key innovation in PLES is that it searches for candidates that reduce the overall uncertainty of a scaling law estimate, instead of optimizing a single objective function. At each iteration, PLES selects the candidate configuration that maximally reduces the uncertainty of the scaling law estimates per unit computational cost, naturally favoring informative small-scale experiments. We evaluate PLES on synthetic benchmarks, surrogate models fitted to real LLM training data, and actual LLM pre-training runs. Across all settings, PLES converges to accurate optimal hyperparameter scaling laws using less than one-tenth of the computational budget required by conventional grid search and other baselines.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CF-AVSS: A Coarse-to-Fine Audio-Visual Speech Separation Framework with Target-Speaker Refinement and Post-Fusion for Real-World AVSE Challenge
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) leverages visual cues to recover target speech from mixtures corrupted by reverberation, noise, and overlapping speakers. We propose a coarse-to-fine two-stage AVSE framework. In the first stage, a progressive SPAV-TFGridNet is extended to two synchronized visual streams to produce visually ordered coarse estimates by progressively suppressing interfering speech while preserving target reverberation and shared background noise. In the second stage, a TFGridNet-based target speaker refinement network takes the original mixture and both coarse estimates as input to further recover target speech and improve signal quality. The coarse and refined estimates are finally combined using development-set-calibrated fusion. On the ISCSLP 2026 Real-World AVSE Challenge, our system tied for first place on Track 1 and ranked second on Track 2 in OVRL, while achieving the lowest CER on both tracks at 12.31% and 14.79%, respectively.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Chronoberg: A 250-Year Diachronic Corpus with Temporal Affective Lexicons for Language Model Analysis
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at operating at scale by leveraging social media and data crawled from the web. Whereas existing corpora are diverse, their frequent lack of long-term temporal structure may however limit an LLM's ability to contextualize semantic and normative evolution of language and to capture diachronic variation. To support the latter, we introduce Chronoberg, a temporally structured corpus of English book texts spanning 250 years, curated from Project Gutenberg and enriched with a variety of temporal annotations. First, the edited nature of books enables us to quantify lexical semantic change through time-sensitive Valence-Arousal-Dominance analysis and to support historically-grounded interpretation. With the lexicons at hand, we demonstrate a need for modern LLM-based tools to better situate their contextualization of sentiment and detection of discriminatory language across various time-periods. In fact, we show how these tools struggle with diachronic shifts in meaning, emphasizing the need for temporally aware training and evaluation pipelines, and positioning Chronoberg as a scalable resource for respective studies. Disclaimer: This paper includes language and display of samples that could be offensive to readers. Open Access: Chronoberg is available publicly on HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/datasets/spaul25/Chronoberg. Code is available at https://github.com/paulsubarna/Chronoberg.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question. A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs, where Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reaches RC4 in only 32.7% of attempts. Across the benchmark, 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fall short of RC4, while all seven models reach RC4 on substantially fewer tasks in all three runs than in at least one. Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure. Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: VDE Bench: Evaluating The Capability of Image Editing Models to Modify Visual Documents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Image editing models can modify visual content through natural language, but editing dense documents requires precise local changes amid tightly coupled text, tables, and layout. We introduce VDE Bench, an evaluation resource for studying instruction-guided editing of Chinese and English document images. VDE Bench contains 3,506 instruction-guided image editing samples, including 1,578 text-region edits and 1,928 table-region edits. The benchmark pairs editing instructions and reference images with annotated editing regions and structured OCR outputs. Its evaluation protocol combines region-level and full-page measurements to assess textual correctness, structural fidelity, and visual content preservation. By focusing on the interaction between local edits and their surrounding document context, VDE Bench complements existing visual text editing benchmarks and provides a resource for diagnosing document-specific editing failures.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Multi-task Neural Diffusion Processes
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Neural diffusion processes provide a scalable, non-Gaussian approach to modelling distributions over functions, but existing formulations are limited to single-task inference and do not capture dependencies across related tasks. We propose multi-task neural diffusion processes (MT-NDPs), an extension that incorporates a task encoder to enable task-conditioned probabilistic regression and few-shot adaptation across related functions. The task encoder extracts a low-dimensional representation from context observations and conditions the diffusion model on this representation, allowing information sharing across tasks while accommodating variable-sized context sets and preserving permutation invariance with respect to the ordering of context observations. We evaluate MT-NDPs through synthetic experiments and two real-world applications involving wind turbine data and school examination outcomes. The results demonstrate improved predictive accuracy relative to single-task diffusion baselines when context observations are available, alongside competitive performance against neural-process and Gaussian-process alternatives. In the wind-energy application, MT-NDPs achieve the lowest average coverage error among the evaluated models at larger context sizes, demonstrating improved predictive uncertainty calibration. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of task-conditioned diffusion models for uncertainty-aware multi-task regression and few-shot adaptation to previously unseen tasks.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Adaptive Duration Model for Text Speech Alignment
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Speech-to-text alignment is a critical component of neural text to speech (TTS) models. Autoregressive TTS models typically use an attention mechanism to learn these alignments on-line, while non-autoregressive end to end TTS models rely on durations extracted from external sources. In this paper, we propose a novel duration prediction framework that can give promising phoneme-level duration distribution with given text. In our experiments, the proposed duration model has more precise prediction and adaptation ability to conditions, compared to previous baseline models. Specifically, it makes a considerable improvement on phoneme-level alignment accuracy and makes the performance of zero-shot TTS models more robust to the mismatch between prompt audio and input audio.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: LLMSurgeon: Diagnosing Data Mixture of Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes their "digital DNA", shaping model behaviors, capabilities, and failure modes. Yet this composition is rarely disclosed, making post-hoc auditing of data combination or provenance difficult. In this work, we formalize Data Mixture Surgery (DMS): given only generated text from a target LLM, estimate the domain-level distribution of its pretraining corpus under a predefined taxonomy. We propose $\textbf{LLMSurgeon}$, a strong framework that casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption. Rather than directly aggregating classifier outputs, LLMSurgeon estimates a calibrated $\textit{soft}$ confusion matrix and solves a constrained inverse problem to correct systematic domain confusion and recover the latent mixture prior. To evaluate, we introduce $\textbf{LLMScan}$, a recipe-verifiable evaluation suite built from open-source LLMs with transparent pretraining mixtures. Across LLMScan, LLMSurgeon recovers domain mixtures with high fidelity under fixed protocols. Our work presents a practical, post-hoc approach for auditing the digital DNA of foundation models without access to their training data.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Harmful Partial Interventions and Benign Leakage in Concept-based Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Artificial intelligence systems deployed in high-risk settings increasingly require models that support meaningful human oversight. Concept-based models (CMs) offer a promising framework by enabling users to inspect and intervene on intermediate, human-understandable concepts. However, concept interventions can counterintuitively worsen downstream predictions, a failure mode we formalise as intervention harm. We distinguish harm after all concepts have been intervened on from harm under partial interventions, the more likely practical use case. Modern CMs often achieve high accuracy by encoding, or leaking, additional task-relevant information in their intermediate concept representations. Recent work argues that such leakage can be benign with respect to intervention harm when concept representations satisfy two conditions: sufficiency and localisation. We prove that these criteria are not sufficient to guarantee that concept interventions improve downstream performance. Across controlled and real-world settings, we find that concept supervision incompleteness is associated with increased intervention harm. Importantly, optimising the model when all concepts are intervened on, a previously proposed leakage mitigation objective, reduces endpoint harm but does not reliably prevent harmful partial corrections. Hence, we introduce a complementary monotonic intervention objective that directly penalises increases in task loss along partial intervention trajectories. Combining endpoint and monotonic intervention training substantially reduces the prevalence and magnitude of partial intervention harm while preserving concept and task predictive performance.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale--accountability tradeoff: larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric. We investigate these predictions through simulations with large language model (LLM) agents. Across five matched pairs of 30-agent simulations, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, exhibiting cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation. We further find that models of different capacity exhibit similar willingness to assume leadership but differ substantially in their exercise of authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more frequently than Luna in matched decision states.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: In-Context Preference-Conditioned Pareto Set Learning from Limited Offline Data
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Multi-objective optimization involves diverse preferences over conflicting objectives. Rather than returning a finite set of trade-off solutions, preference-conditioned Pareto set learning seeks to map a specified preference directly to a corresponding Pareto optimal solution. Yet in many real-world scenarios, optimization must proceed offline without further objective evaluations, leaving only a limited static dataset that sparsely covers the decision and objective spaces. Existing methods either optimize separately for each preference or train a problem-specific Pareto solution model, requiring repeated search across preferences or repeated training across problems. We introduce in-context preference-conditioned Pareto set learning (ICPSL), a framework that amortizes both preference-wise solution search and problem-specific model construction. ICPSL pretrains a foundation-style hypernetwork on a large and diverse set of synthetic prior data. Given the offline observations of an unseen problem, the pretrained hypernetwork learns to generate a problem-specific, preference-conditioned Pareto solution model in a single forward pass. The generated model can then be reused to predict solutions for arbitrary preferences without problem-specific training or preference-wise search. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show that ICPSL produces high-quality Pareto solutions while providing substantial speedups in problem-specific solution-model construction.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail to Use Available Evidence
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Web search allows LLMs to access up-to-date information, but it remains unclear why they sometimes produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available. To study this problem, we construct temporal facts whose values changed after the models' training cutoffs. We evaluate one proprietary model under deployed web search and six open-weight model configurations under controlled retrieval. We find that models often answer from search snippets without opening the source pages, which is associated with higher rates of outdated answers and unfaithful citations. Our controlled experiments and layer-wise analysis reveal a gap between the availability of evidence and its effective use. Even when retrieved evidence influences internal predictions, models may still favour outdated information in their final answers. We hope these findings will help advance research on the reliable use of retrieved evidence in search-augmented LLMs.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Gradual Probabilistic Lambda Calculus
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Probabilistic programming languages extend ordinary programming languages with the ability to sample values from probability distributions. Type systems can establish invariants of such programs, for instance by assigning to a program a distribution over types that specifies the probability of each kind of outcome. However, adopting such a type discipline can be cumbersome or overly conservative.
  Gradual typing addresses this problem by supporting a smooth transition between static and dynamic checking, and has been successfully applied for languages with different constructs and type abstractions. Nevertheless, its benefits have never been explored in the context of probabilistic languages.
  In this work, we present and formalize GLANG, a gradual source probabilistic lambda calculus. GLANG includes a binary probabilistic choice operator and allows programmers to gradually introduce/remove static type---and probability---annotations. The static semantics of GLANG heavily relies on the notion of probabilistic couplings, as required for defining several relations, such as consistency, precision, and consistent transitivity. The dynamic semantics of GLANG is given via elaboration to the target language TLANG, which features a distribution-based semantics interpreting programs as probability distributions over final values. Regarding the language metatheory, we establish that TLANG---and therefore also GLANG---is type safe and satisfies two of the so-called refined criteria for gradual languages, namely, that it is a conservative extension of a fully static variant and that it satisfies (a restricted form of) the gradual guarantee, behaving smoothly with respect to type precision. The metatheory is mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Bidirectional Elaborators à la Carte
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines.
  We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-Löf type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-Löf type theory.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Enhancing Knowledge Density via Hierarchical Context Pruning for Retrieval-Augmented Repository-Level Code Completion
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced repository-level code completion by retrieving external code snippets, API documentation, or type definitions to expand the model's contextual awareness. However, under the finite token budget of the context window, existing retrieval-augmented methods often saturate the budget with highly similar or even redundant code, which not only wastes tokens but also suppresses critical cross-file dependencies, preventing synergistic interaction between semantically similar reference snippets and cross-file dependency definitions. Therefore, further gains are limited by low knowledge density in the retrieved context rather than by model capacity. We propose SaraCoder, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances knowledge density via hierarchical context pruning under a fixed context budget. A Hierarchical Feature Optimization module prunes an over-complete candidate pool in four stages. The freed tokens are then allocated to an External-Aware Identifier Disambiguator, which selectively injects only the most necessary cross-file dependency definitions. SaraCoder transforms context construction into a budget-aware optimization problem, balancing reference snippets and cross-file dependencies to build a context that is both knowledge-dense and semantically complete. Experiments on CrossCodeEval and RepoEval-Updated, across multiple backbone code LLMs, show that SaraCoder consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines such as GraphCoder and Repocoder in both code-level and identifier-level metrics, without increasing token usage, and yields synergistic gains when combined with other cross-file methods.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Negative and Fractional Types in the Fidelity Framework
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Programs routinely create temporary data, retain state and revisit earlier results. Negative and fractional types benefit those activities in a type-resolved account of computation. Negative values redirect evaluation. Fractional values introduce value-specific auxiliary data and discharge it after a computation restores the required value. We develop both as first-class computational forms in our Clef design, using Chen and Sabry's directed, value-indexed calculus and distinguishing James and Sabry's logic-variable search interpretation. Our Program Semantic Graph retains their value identities and resource uses, enabling Composer to preserve their behavior through MLIR operations and native realization. In this paper, a negative-type counter and a fractional workspace calculation demonstrate the two constructions. Local proofs establish preservation of matching and independent resource discharge. Dimensional inference and proof terms supply premises through our four verification tiers. The applications connect deferred reverse computation to gradient calculations without an activation tape, and checked inverse steps to in-memory event recovery. A finite reconstruction horizon governs the exchange between storage and recomputation. We derive its error recurrence and show where Urschel's elimination-growth bounds can support a realized inverse step. Bayesian updates and quantum circuits supply further computational cases, including temporary workspace, measurement and a worked adiabatic schedule. Exact matching, bounded reconstruction and physical realization retain their respective contracts. The resulting architecture makes the information needed to run, reverse or complete a computation available to the compiler. Libraries can expose these operations through familiar interfaces while their retained structure supports unboxed execution and differential compilation across targets.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Fixed-Point Scaffolding in the Clef Programming Language
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Native compilation changes how a program represents values and performs operations from processor to processor. In our view, proofs that justify source-level decisions must remain connected to those changes. We develop fixed-point scaffolding for this continuity in Clef and our Composer compiler. Our Program Semantic Graph retains types, joint constraints and proof dependencies. A thin MLIR middle end witnesses their settled consequences for native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA realization. The account connects nanopass traversal with preservation contracts, structural theorems and adjoint interfaces between reasoning modes. Four verification tiers organize automatic inference and reusable domain and system proofs, with probabilistic relations admitted at Tier 4. Established lower-tier facts can directly support richer derivations. We state conditions for composing lowering contracts and assembling compatible program segments, then show how their dependencies govern differential compilation after an edit. A worked foreign-call boundary follows source ranges through argument marshaling, the actual call and return conversion. Current FFI mechanisms bind checking evidence to those witnessed operations. A recent paper from Urschel provides elimination-growth bounds that supply a quantitative example. Reusable premises inform representation and error contracts that retain their sampling, arithmetic and exceptional-path assumptions. A further example admits value-indexed pairing through ordinary MLIR operations, connecting this scaffold to negative and fractional types. Together these constructions explain how a thin middle end can carry the consequences of rich source proofs into unboxed computation graphs. Integrity and efficiency share the same retained evidence. It justifies native realizations and identifies which analyses, proofs and lowered fragments remain reusable during development.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Decidable By Construction: Design-Time Verification for Truly Fearless Systems
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Concurrency, parallelism and distributed execution become truly fearless when the compiler tracks wait-for edges, proves multi-threaded work is sound and preserves distributed boundary contracts. In this design, our Composer compiler preserves proofs while lowering Clef directly to native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA code, without translation through C or vendor APIs. Our Program Semantic Graph retains the values, relationships and premises that justify BAREWire's unboxed boundary contracts. And C & C++ interfacing is an explicit marshaling boundary, with proofs tied to actual arguments, conversions and returned values. Four verification tiers connect an account of our design. Tier 1 supplies structural inference, founded on principal dimensional types. Tier 2 generates and checks local arithmetic, representation, and computational integrity at the node level. Tier 3 instantiates reusable domain and system lemmas, including distributed proofs supported by Iris, Actris and Aneris. Tiers 1-3 require no developer annotations, with a quotation based lemma library design to extend coverage as use cases expand. Tier 4 admits computational and probabilistic relational proofs, with project annotations identifying the required relations. We extend the same library direction toward recognizing relational constructions from hypergraph structure. A formal composition rule connects arithmetic, ownership, protocol and realization evidence. Our worked distributed reduction preserves one specified result across concurrent workers, reordered arrivals and boundary mappings. Its probabilistic extension carries worker and conversion error with an explicit failure budget. With recent work by Urschel, we show bounds supply a relevant source of reusable proof terms. These constructions make verification a core engineering discipline for truly fearless programs and systems across a variety of hardware targets.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Dimensional Type Systems and Deterministic Memory Management
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: We present a dimensional type system whose annotations remain available through the stages that require them, allowing numeric representation and deterministic memory management to be resolved within a single Program Semantic Graph (PSG). Based on Andrew Kennedy's Units of Measure, dimensions constrain admissible operations and the application of domain laws, forming our Native Type Universe (NTU). Range analysis combines those constraints with values, guards, and declared boundaries. A covering representation then determines word width and memory footprint, which participate in allocation and transfer decisions alongside lifetime and target constraints. Our Dimensional Type System (DTS) extends Hindley-Milner inference with abelian-group unification. Within that algebraic fragment, inference is decidable and admits principal types. Measures form part of source-level type identity, while numeric width and storage layout are coeffects resolved from context. A known range that exceeds every available representation produces an error at representation commitment. During program elaboration, unresolved facts can remain pending while further context is supplied. Deterministic Memory Management (DMM) uses the same graph to relate escape paths to storage lifetimes. Closure capture, return, and by-reference use supply different lifetime requirements. Allocation follows the lifetime classification and the platform's declared storage capabilities. Our unique implementation of a posit quire illustrates the interaction: exact accumulation requires a suitable numeric format, adequate capacity, and storage that persists across the accumulation. We also examine how these constraints would apply to automatic differentiation. A shared graph would allow language services to present dimensional resolution and proof status alongside the reasons for representation and placement decisions.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: The Program Hypergraph: Multi-Way Relational Structure for Geometric Algebra, Spatial Compute, and Physics-Aware Compilation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Source code organizes a program as expressions and declarations, which a compiler can represent as an abstract syntax tree (AST). Some compilers introduce a further abstraction of the computation as a graph. Nodes represent operations, while connections record how values pass between them and how execution proceeds. Yet these connections can leave the full scope of conditions governing a computation implicit. Developers may then need defensive checks, rely on compiler hacks, pragmas, and implementation-specific code to maintain those conditions as the program evolves. Our thesis is that a hypergraph more faithfully represents complex computation across all targets by making joint constraints inherent to its structure, with an overall less burdensome design-time API. Our Program Hypergraph (PHG) extends our Semantic Graph with relations that connect across an operation's participants, their dependencies, and the invariants they must preserve. Joint resolution in the graph guides lowering into standard Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks intrinsic to the graph discharge applicable proof obligations. Supporting information remains available until the decisions that require it are complete. As a primary benefit, verification follows from the rules used to construct and transform the graph. For properties established this way before execution, the generated program needs no added runtime checks, no 'boxing' or 'tagging' or other managed runtime support. We develop this account through geometric algebra, shared-memory capacity, and spatial placement, distinguishing structural guarantees from numerical and resource obligations that require further evidence. The proposed integration makes the same information available at design-time, so engineers can inspect the consequences of a choice before it becomes an implementation constraint.
